title: Alidu and the Melting Ice Block

pages.text: On a hot afternoon, Alidu and Mariam bought an ice block from Auntie Sherifa. An ice block is a frozen bag of clean drinking water. The water inside was hard and cold, like a stone. “It is ice,” said Alidu. “Ice is water in a solid form.”
sentences: On a hot afternoon, Alidu and Mariam bought an ice block from Auntie Sherifa.
An ice block is a frozen bag of clean drinking water.
The water inside was hard and cold, like a stone.
“It is ice,” said Alidu.
“Ice is water in a solid form.”
pages.alt: At a sunny Ghanaian roadside table, smiling Auntie Sherifa lifts a frosty clear frozen water bag from a blue cooler box for Alidu and Mariam.

pages.text: They put the frozen bag on a plate in the sun. After ten minutes, drops of water formed around it. After half an hour, the ice had gone soft and the plate was wet. “It is melting!” said Mariam.
sentences: They put the frozen bag on a plate in the sun.
After ten minutes, drops of water formed around it.
After half an hour, the ice had gone soft and the plate was wet.
“It is melting!” said Mariam.
pages.alt: On a sunlit wooden veranda table, Alidu and Mariam lean in curiously watching a half-melted clear bag of ice sitting in a puddle of water on an enamel plate.

pages.text: Soon, most of the ice had turned into water. “The warmth from the sun and the air made the ice melt,” said their teacher. “Ice is a solid. Melted ice is a liquid.”
sentences: Soon, most of the ice had turned into water.
“The warmth from the sun and the air made the ice melt,” said their teacher.
“Ice is a solid.
Melted ice is a liquid.”
pages.alt: In the bright classroom, their male teacher points to the enamel plate now holding mostly clear liquid water with a tiny sliver of ice while Alidu and Mariam watch.

pages.text: Their teacher told them one more thing. “When water is heated more, it turns into a gas called water vapour. We cannot see it. So water can be a solid, a liquid or a gas.”
sentences: Their teacher told them one more thing.
“When water is heated more, it turns into a gas called water vapour.
We cannot see it.
So water can be a solid, a liquid or a gas.”
pages.alt: On a classroom demonstration table stand three items in a neat row—a bowl of solid ice blocks, a glass of clear water, and a warm cup with faint rising mist—as the teacher gestures.

pages.text: “A solid keeps its shape,” said the teacher. “A liquid takes the shape of its container. A gas spreads out to fill the space.” Mariam poured water from a bottle into a bowl and watched it take the bowl’s shape.
sentences: “A solid keeps its shape,” said the teacher.

pages.alt: Mariam carefully pouring clear water from a tall narrow bottle into a wide round bowl on the desk while Alidu and the teacher smile and observe.

pages.text: Alidu asked, “Can melted ice become ice again?” “Yes,” said the teacher. “If the water is cooled enough, it freezes. Heating and cooling can change water from one state to another.” The children wrote this in their notebooks.

pages.alt: Alidu and Mariam sitting at their wooden classroom desk happily sketching ice blocks and water drops in their open exercise books with pencils.

activities.question: What happened to the ice in the sun?
What does a liquid do?
options: It takes the shape of its container

items: More heat makes vapour, a gas.

activities.definition: To change from a solid to a liquid when warmed.

glossary.definition: Changing from a solid to a liquid because of heat.
Something that keeps its shape, such as ice or a stone.
Something that flows and takes the shape of its container, such as water.
